messages.author: c102ef7f5617067f
messages.subject: Can I take these measurements in seewave?
parts:
I have been using Raven Pro to take measurement of bird calls. I'm considering using seewave instead. In general, can seewave take similar measurements of bird calls that can be taken in Raven Pro?

More specifically, how easy is it to collect these measurements of bird calls in seewave:

duration of a specific call
frequency at start of call
frequency at end of call
maximum frequency of a specific call 
time of maximum frequency
frequency range of specific call 
number calls in a recording

messages.author: d91178de15999ecf
messages.subject: Re: [seewave] Can I take these measurements in seewave?
parts:
Hi Ross,

I use seewave for all of those measurements, with the possible exception of the "number of calls in a recording" because seewave is a bit slow when dealing with really large files (mine are all > 30 min).

I use a series of R scripts to extract these measures. First I manually specify the start and stop times of all notes (I work with chickadee songs), then I have R + seewave calculate note/song lengths. Next I'd use dfreq() to calculate dominant frequencies measured at different times across the note and use these numbers to get the freq at the start and stop of the note. You could also use this to get the maximum freq and the corresponding time of that freq (but that would be the maximum dominant freq, which may not be what you want. You could also use spec() and manually select the maximum freq from the power spectrum). From dfreq() you could also get the freq range by going from the minimum value to the maximum, but, once again, this somewhat depends on what kind of maximum frequency you want to measure.

Bear in mind that if you're unfamiliar with R, seewave can be a bit challenging at first so you should plan on some time invested to get things figured out. But once you've invested the time, it's amazing how automated you can make everything! Right now I use seewave to cut out my songs from the recording (through SoX), manually record the length of each note, and then automatically record frequency, and relative amplitude of all notes. I even have it set up to print out a series of spectrograms with the measurements drawn on them so I can verify that everything is measured correctly.

If you really get into the programming, you can even take advantage of multicore processing to speed things up, somewhat :)

Steffi

messages.author: e14cfb57d640984d
messages.subject: Re: [seewave] Can I take these measurements in seewave?
parts:
I've also found seewave extremely useful for measurements.

One comment on some of the measurements of energy and duration: measurements can be made more precise and repeatable if you look at something like the inner 90% quantile of the energy distribution. In the case of energy, this can also help with "edge" effects, where the frequency given by dfreq() may not be part of the signal.

For more detail on this phenomenon see http://www.birds.cornell.edu/brp/research/algorithm/automated-and-robust-measurement-of-signal-features

I mention this because Raven has built-in facilities for doing measurements in this robust way, and seewave doesn't. That's the only difference I can think of. I personally choose seewave whenever I can, due to the convenience of being able to script it!

best,
jesse

messages.author: e14cfb57d640984d
messages.subject: Re: [seewave] Can I take these measurements in seewave?
parts:
Hi Steffi,

dfreq() seems to me to work pretty well even on somewhat noisy recordings. But you could have a version of it which only looked at the inner 90% of the energy per time slice, and that might help it be a little more robust in noisy situations.

I think what Cortopassi is actually suggesting is creating an aggregate power distribution as a function of frequency for the entire frequency band of interest, taking the inner 90% or so of the energy, and then computing measures such as mean, standard deviation, skewness, etc. on this distribution. These would be single measures, rather than vectors as we get from dfreq(), and they ought to be fairly robust to small variations in where the frequency band of interest is specified to be, which seem to be kind of inevitable when drawing boxes on spectrograms.

The approach has been coded up in a MATLAB toolkit called Acoustat, which has shown up in some publications. I believe the approach was originated by Kurt Fristrup. So those might be good google terms if you want to dig in further. I do not know what the licensing situation is with Acoustat, but if anybody is interested in porting the core algorithms to R/seewave, I could probably put them in touch with someone who would know about that.

Best,
Jesse Ross
Research Analyst
Bioacoustics Research Program
Cornell Lab of Ornithology

On 13-11-15 04:01 PM, Jesse Ross wrote:
Hi Steffi,

dfreq() seems to me to work pretty well even on somewhat noisy recordings. But you could have a version of it which only looked at the inner 90% of the energy per time slice, and that might help it be a little more robust in noisy situations.

I think what Cortopassi is actually suggesting is creating an aggregate power distribution as a function of frequency for the entire frequency band of interest, taking the inner 90% or so of the energy, and then computing measures such as mean, standard deviation, skewness, etc. on this distribution. These would be single measures, rather than vectors as we get from dfreq(), and they ought to be fairly robust to small variations in where the frequency band of interest is specified to be, which seem to be kind of inevitable when drawing boxes on spectrograms.

The approach has been coded up in a MATLAB toolkit called Acoustat, which has shown up in some publications. I believe the approach was originated by Kurt Fristrup. So those might be good google terms if you want to dig in further. I do not know what the licensing situation is with Acoustat, but if anybody is interested in porting the core algorithms to R/seewave, I could probably put them in touch with someone who would know about that.

Best,

On 13-11-15 01:22 PM, Jesse Ross wrote:
I've also found seewave extremely useful for measurements.

One comment on some of the measurements of energy and duration: measurements can be made more precise and repeatable if you look at something like the inner 90% quantile of the energy distribution. In the case of energy, this can also help with "edge" effects, where the frequency given by dfreq() may not be part of the signal.

For more detail on this phenomenon see http://www.birds.cornell.edu/brp/research/algorithm/automated-and-robust-measurement-of-signal-features

I mention this because Raven has built-in facilities for doing measurements in this robust way, and seewave doesn't. That's the only difference I can think of. I personally choose seewave whenever I can, due to the convenience of being able to script it!

On Thu, Nov 14, 2013 at 12:23 PM, Stefanie LaZerte <laz...@unbc.ca> wrote:
Hi Ross,

I use seewave for all of those measurements, with the possible exception of the "number of calls in a recording" because seewave is a bit slow when dealing with really large files (mine are all > 30 min).

I use a series of R scripts to extract these measures. First I manually specify the start and stop times of all notes (I work with chickadee songs), then I have R + seewave calculate note/song lengths. Next I'd use dfreq() to calculate dominant frequencies measured at different times across the note and use these numbers to get the freq at the start and stop of the note. You could also use this to get the maximum freq and the corresponding time of that freq (but that would be the maximum dominant freq, which may not be what you want. You could also use spec() and manually select the maximum freq from the power spectrum). From dfreq() you could also get the freq range by going from the minimum value to the maximum, but, once again, this somewhat depends on what kind of maximum frequency you want to measure.

Bear in mind that if you're unfamiliar with R, seewave can be a bit challenging at first so you should plan on some time invested to get things figured out. But once you've invested the time, it's amazing how automated you can make everything! Right now I use seewave to cut out my songs from the recording (through SoX), manually record the length of each note, and then automatically record frequency, and relative amplitude of all notes. I even have it set up to print out a series of spectrograms with the measurements drawn on them so I can verify that everything is measured correctly.

If you really get into the programming, you can even take advantage of multicore processing to speed things up, somewhat :)
